glance.label: Main Idea
glance.html: The Elder calls the church to walk in truth and love, to abide in the doctrine of Christ, and to refuse support to deceivers who deny that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh.

glance.label: Setting
glance.html: The writer calls himself “the Elder,” most likely the apostle John, and writes to “the elect lady and her children” (1:1), most likely a local congregation and its members. Traveling teachers depended on believers’ hospitality, which made the question of whom to welcome urgent.

glance.label: Key Verse
glance.html: “Whoever transgresses and does not abide in the doctrine of Christ does not have God. He who abides in the doctrine of Christ has both the Father and the Son.” (2 John 1:9, NKJV)

cards.title: The Heart of the Chapter
cards.html:
Second John is one of the shortest books in the Bible, and its first four verses are full of one word. The Elder loves the church “in truth,” along with “all those who have known the truth,” because of “the truth which abides in us and will be with us forever” (1:1–2). Truth here is no set of ideas held at arm’s length. It is the truth revealed in and about Jesus, who called Himself “the truth” (John 14:6), and it lives in His people.

That truth has a shape, and its shape is love. John rejoices to find some of the church’s children “walking in truth” (1:4), then pleads for the old commandment “that we love one another” (1:5). He defines love plainly: “that we walk according to His commandments” (1:6). John never asks the church to balance truth against love. Truth is the life in which love is lived.

Then comes the danger. “Many deceivers have gone out into the world who do not confess Jesus Christ as coming in the flesh” (1:7). To deny the real incarnation is to lose God Himself, for whoever leaves the doctrine of Christ “does not have God,” while whoever abides in it “has both the Father and the Son” (1:9). So the church must not welcome such teachers or wish them well in their work (1:10–11). Even this warning comes from love, and the letter ends with John’s longing to see them “face to face, that our joy may be full” (1:12).

cards.title: Chapter Sections
cards.html:
2 John 1:1–3 — The Elder Greets the Elect Lady in Truth and Love

The Elder greets the elect lady and her children, whom he and all who know the truth love because the truth abides in them. Grace, mercy and peace come from the Father and from Jesus Christ, the Son of the Father, “in truth and love” (1:3), the two words that govern the whole letter.

2 John 1:4–6 — Walking in Truth and in Love

John rejoices over believers walking in truth and urges the commandment they have had from the beginning, to love one another. Love is not left vague: it is walking according to God’s commandments.

2 John 1:7–9 — Abide in the Doctrine of Christ

Many deceivers deny that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh, so the church must guard itself and not lose what has been worked for. Leaving the doctrine of Christ means not having God, while abiding in it means having both the Father and the Son.

2 John 1:10–11 — Do Not Receive the Teacher Who Denies Christ

The church is not to receive into the house or greet a teacher who comes without the doctrine of Christ, because such a welcome shares in his evil work. The command concerns support and endorsement of Christ-denying teaching, not ordinary kindness toward people who believe differently.

2 John 1:12–13 — Hope of Speaking Face to Face

John has much more to say but would rather speak face to face, so that their joy may be full. The children of the elect sister send greetings, a likely picture of one congregation greeting another.

cards.title: Why This Chapter Matters
cards.html:
Second John shows that truth and love cannot be pulled apart. A church that keeps the truth without love grows cold, and a church that keeps a love detached from truth loses Christ. John holds both together because both come from Him.

The letter also shows why the identity of Jesus matters. The line John draws is not over every disagreement but over whether Jesus Christ truly came in the flesh, and he says that this question decides whether a person has God at all (1:7, 9). Finally, it shows that welcome is a kind of partnership. Believers can be kind to everyone, but they must not lend their homes and blessing to work that leads people away from Christ.

cards.title: Key Themes to Watch For
cards.html:
Truth that abides. Truth lives in believers and will be with them forever (1:1–4).

Love that obeys. Love is walking according to God’s commandments, the command heard from the beginning (1:5–6).

The incarnation. The decisive confession is Jesus Christ “coming in the flesh” (1:7).

Abiding. Remaining in the doctrine of Christ means having the Father and the Son (1:2, 9).

Joy in fellowship. The letter moves between John’s great joy and his hope of full joy face to face (1:4, 12).

cards.title: Key Words & Concepts
cards.html:
The Elder. The writer’s title for himself (1:1). He is most likely the apostle John, known to the church as an older leader with pastoral authority.

The elect lady. Most likely a local congregation, with “her children” its members (1:1) and her “elect sister” another church (1:13). Some take her as an individual Christian woman and her family.

Antichrist. Here anyone who denies Jesus’ coming in the flesh (1:7). John teaches elsewhere that many antichrists are already present (1 John 2:18).

Transgresses. The NKJV reads a word meaning to step beyond, while many manuscripts read goes ahead (1:9). Either way it describes leaving the teaching of Christ.

The doctrine of Christ. The apostolic teaching about Christ, especially His Person and incarnation (1:9–10).

Receive and greet. Welcoming a traveling teacher and wishing him well meant supporting his ministry (1:10–11; compare 3 John 5–8). John forbids that support for those who deny Christ.

culture.title: HONOR || Through His Eyes
culture.statement:
Value Statement

Relationships are protected when we ascribe heaven’s value to the people around us. Like Jesus, we choose to interact with people, not as they deserve, but according to their God given value.
culture.label: Living It in 2 John 1
culture.html:
John addresses this church as “the elect lady” (v. 1). Before he says anything else about them, he names what God has done: God chose them. He tells them he loves them in truth, that believers who have never met them love them too, and that he rejoiced greatly over what he found among them (vv. 1, 4). Even his instruction comes as a request: “And now I plead with you, lady” (v. 5). John had the authority to give orders, yet he spoke to the church according to what they are in God’s sight. Honor sees people as God sees them and speaks to them that way, even when there is something serious to say.

The letter also shows what honor does and does not require. John forbids the church to receive or greet a teacher who denies Christ in a way that would help his message spread (vv. 10–11). Honor does not mean endorsing what someone teaches or giving their ministry a platform. We may sometimes need to refuse a teaching, decline an invitation, or withhold endorsement from a ministry. Honor still governs how we respond. We can speak plainly and establish necessary boundaries without mockery, contempt, or forgetting the God-given value of the person involved.

culture.title: FELLOWSHIP || Assembly Required
culture.statement:
Value Statement

We are united by our pursuit of the Lord. We come together to discover His heart and partner with His will. Breaking bread is optional, but strongly encouraged.
culture.label: Living It in 2 John 1
culture.html:
John’s love for this church did not depend on shared background, location, or personality. “All those who have known the truth” love them, “because of the truth which abides in us” (vv. 1–2). That is what unites the people of God. Believers come from different histories, places, tastes, and opinions. What makes them one body is that they pursue the same Lord and share the same truth about Him. A fellowship held together only by friendship or preference is fragile. A fellowship gathered around Jesus Christ has something deeper holding it together, and it reaches beyond one congregation to “the children of your elect sister” (v. 13) in churches we may never visit.

John could have tried to say everything in this letter. Instead he hoped to come and be with them, “that our joy may be full” (v. 12). Christian fellowship is more than exchanging information. When believers gather, they pray with one another, hear the Word side by side, worship as one body, and share life around a table. A letter or a screen can carry news, and online services are a gift when we cannot be present, but neither fully replaces that shared life. Scripture calls believers not to forsake “the assembling of ourselves together” (Hebrews 10:25). John’s longing to be with this church shows why gathering is worth protecting rather than casually neglecting.

culture.title: GENEROSITY || It's Not Ours Anyway
culture.statement:
Value Statement

We recognize that every resource we’ve been given comes from our generous Father. We choose to be just like Dad, and give as He leads.
culture.label: Living It in 2 John 1
culture.html:
In the first-century church, hospitality was one of the main ways believers gave. A home, a meal, and provisions for the road kept traveling teachers moving from church to church and carried the gospel with them (3 John 5–8). John’s instruction in verses 10–11 shows that this kind of support had consequences. Receiving a traveling teacher gave him resources, credibility, and help on his way, so the same support that advanced the truth could also advance a lie. Whoever welcomed and supported a teacher who denied Christ “shares in his evil deeds” (v. 11). This does not make every act of hospitality an endorsement. It means believers should consider what their support advances.

Because every resource we have comes from our Father, our generosity should be directed by His truth, wisdom, and leading. The Holy Spirit is the Spirit of truth (John 16:13), and He does not lead believers to support a message that denies the Son. This should not make us stingy or suspicious. The same principle works in the other direction. When we give to the house of God, support missionaries, or open our homes to those who serve the Lord faithfully, we “become fellow workers for the truth” (3 John 8). Generosity joins us to the work it supports, and that is a privilege.

culture.title: We are People of the Word
culture.statement:
Value Statement

The Holy Bible is the only infallible and final authority for Christian faith and life. The Holy Scriptures are timeless, inerrant and are to be read personally, discerned corporately, and walked out in community. We interpret all Scripture through the life and teachings of Jesus, trusting Holy Spirit to reveal truth and transform us as we submit ourselves fully to God’s revealed Word.
culture.label: Living It in 2 John 1
culture.html:
John measures everything by what the church received at the beginning. The commandment is the one “we have had from the beginning” (v. 5). The test for any teacher is whether he brings “the doctrine of Christ” (vv. 9–10), with the truth that Jesus Christ came in the flesh at its center (v. 7). Jesus is the center of all Scripture, and 2 John shows why the truth about Him must stay at the center of how we read it. Spirit-filled believers welcome Holy Spirit’s voice and expect Him to speak. He leads believers deeper into the truth God has revealed about Christ, not away from it. Every teaching, prophetic word, spiritual impression, or claimed revelation must be weighed in light of Scripture and the truth about Jesus Christ.

John’s instructions address believers together, reminding us that discerning truth is not merely an individual responsibility. We benefit from testing teaching in the light of Scripture alongside mature believers and trusted spiritual leaders, especially when something sounds new. Reading the Bible personally remains essential, and discernment is strengthened in community. The goal is never only to be correct. The believers who brought John joy were “walking in truth” (v. 4). Truth is meant to be walked out, not simply known or defended.

culture.title: Communication
culture.statement:
Value Statement

We “real talk” because we desire real relationships built on trust. We have 100% of our conversations, choosing to be authentic, honest, and open with one another. Awkward today, stronger tomorrow.
culture.label: Living It in 2 John 1
culture.html:
John speaks to this church about both joy and concern. He tells them plainly what brought him joy: some of their children are walking in truth (v. 4). He tells them just as plainly about the danger they face: deceivers are at work, and “This is a deceiver and an antichrist” (v. 7). Then he says, “Look to yourselves” (v. 8). Having 100% of our conversations includes both encouragement and necessary correction. It means telling someone what we see God doing in them and telling them honestly when we see something that could cost them what God has built. That kind of communication is truthful and honoring, and it comes from love for the person.

John also had “many things” he chose not to put in writing, and he hoped to “speak face to face” (v. 12). Sensitive or difficult conversations deserve that kind of personal attention rather than being avoided or handled entirely through text messages. Those conversations may be awkward today. They make relationships stronger tomorrow.

sections.title: The Elder Greets the Elect Lady in Truth and Love

items.title: Truth Is the Reason for Love, Not Its Rival (2 John 1:1–3)
items.html: Four times in three verses John ties love to truth. He loves this household “in truth” (v. 1); “all who know the truth” love them too (v. 1); he loves them “for the sake of the truth which abides in us” (v. 2); and God’s grace stays with us “in truth and love” (v. 3). Our culture assumes that truth divides and love includes, so love must sometimes set truth aside. John sees it the other way around: truth is what turns strangers into family. Believers who have never met this woman or this church love her because the same truth lives in both. The deepest, most unbreakable bonds between people do not come from shared hobbies, blood, or culture; they come from the mutual indwelling of the eternal Truth. When the Spirit of truth in one believer recognizes the Spirit of truth in another, a lasting fellowship is forged. The truth makes true love possible. Love built on shared tastes or shared history frays; love built on the truth that “will be with us forever” (v. 2) lasts as long as its foundation. A church that guards the truth is guarding the root of its love.
items.q: Four times in three verses John ties love to truth.

items.title: The DNA Double Helix of Truth and Love (2 John 1:1–3)
items.html: In three verses “truth” appears four times and “love” twice, wound together like the two strands of DNA. Isolate truth from love, and you get a sword that only cuts and condemns, truth weaponized into legalism. Isolate love from truth, and you get a shapeless sentimentality that tolerates deception. Sentimentality without truth deceives; truth without love destroys. John binds them together for good: true love is always rooted in truth, and eternal truth always shows itself as love. Discipling others means refusing the cultural pressure to divorce the two, and showing how to wield the sword of truth with the heartbeat of love.
items.q: In three verses “truth” appears four times and “love” twice, wound together like the two strands of DNA.

items.title: Truth Is the Atmosphere of the Kingdom (2 John 1:1–3)
items.html: The section moves from the elder to the lady, binds them together through an inward reality, the indwelling truth, and then opens heaven to pour out grace, mercy, and peace. Truth here is not just a subject we study; it is the atmosphere of the kingdom of God. A fish does not think about water; it simply lives in it. For the believer, truth is the environment in which we breathe, love, and receive grace.
items.q: The section moves from the elder to the lady, binds them together through an inward reality, the indwelling truth, and then opens heaven to pour out grace, mercy, and peace.

items.title: The Guardrails of Grace (2 John 1:3)
items.html: “Grace, mercy, and peace” are the ultimate freedom and favor of God, and John immediately walls them in with “truth and love.” Grace without truth turns into license. Grace without love turns into cold, religious mechanics. The ecosystem of blessing requires both.
items.q: “Grace, mercy, and peace” are the ultimate freedom and favor of God, and John immediately walls them in with “truth and love.”

items.title: Five Times “Truth” Before One Word of Warning (2 John 1:1–4, 7)
items.html: “Truth” appears five times in verses 1–4, and the deceivers do not appear until verse 7. Before John says a word about the danger at the door, he fills the house: the truth they know, the truth that abides, the grace that will stay, the children walking in truth. People are protected from counterfeits by long familiarity with what is real, not by a steady diet of warnings. Churches and families that hear more about error than about Christ grow anxious and brittle rather than discerning. Lead people into the beauty of the truth first, and the warnings will have something to protect.
items.q: “Truth” appears five times in verses 1–4, and the deceivers do not appear until verse 7.

sections.title: Walking in Truth and in Love

items.title: One Road With Three Names (2 John 1:4–6)
items.html: “Walk” appears three times in three verses: walking “in truth” (v. 4), walking “according to His commandments” (v. 6a), and walking “in it,” in love (v. 6b). Truth, commandment, and love are not three paths a believer chooses among; they are one road described three ways. Jesus called Himself “the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6), and in this passage truth, obedience, and love all turn out to be the same walk with Him. A church that walks in truth without love has left the road, and so has a church that walks in love without obedience. The Christian life is not a lecture to attend but a road to walk, one ordinary step after another, at home as much as in church.
items.q: “Walk” appears three times in three verses: walking “in truth” (v. 4), walking “according to His commandments” (v. 6a), and walking “in it,” in love (v. 6b).

items.title: Not a Circle but a Spiral Staircase (2 John 1:4–6)
items.html: The section moves from observation (I found your children walking), to appeal (I ask that we love), to definition (love is walking in His commandments). Put together, verses 4–6 make a loop. How do we know we are in the truth? Because we obey. What do we obey? The command to love. What is love? Walking in obedience. This is not circular reasoning; it is a spiral staircase. Every act of obedience deepens our capacity to love, and every deepening of love quickens our desire to obey.
items.q: The section moves from observation (I found your children walking), to appeal (I ask that we love), to definition (love is walking in His commandments).

items.title: Truth That Is Caught and Walked (2 John 1:4–6)
items.html: John’s joy over the children walking in truth reveals the true test of a ministry’s or a parent’s vitality: not what they themselves believe, but whether their truth was real enough to be caught, owned, and walked in by the next generation. A truth merely taught can be discarded; a truth lived and walked is contagious.
items.q: John’s joy over the children walking in truth reveals the true test of a ministry’s or a parent’s vitality: not what they themselves believe, but whether their truth was real enough to be caught, owned, and walked in by the next generation.

items.title: Walking Is a Series of Controlled Falls (2 John 1:4–6)
items.html: Walking is steady, rhythmic, forward motion, and it requires balance; physically, it is a series of controlled falls, shifting weight from one leg to the other. Spiritually, we shift our weight between receiving truth and giving love, and so keep moving forward. A Christian is not someone who merely stands on the truth, but someone who walks in it.
items.q: Walking is steady, rhythmic, forward motion, and it requires balance; physically, it is a series of controlled falls, shifting weight from one leg to the other.

items.title: The Devastating Simplicity of the Ancient Path (2 John 1:4–6)
items.html: In a world that loves theological novelty, John drastically simplifies what God requires. He gathers the commands into one mandate: walk in love, which is obedience. That strips away the religious complications we love to build around faith. The ancient path is brilliantly, devastatingly simple: obey God by loving others.
items.q: In a world that loves theological novelty, John drastically simplifies what God requires.

items.title: Love Is the First Line of Defense (2 John 1:5–7)
items.html: John moves straight from “that we love one another” (v. 5) to “For many deceivers have gone out into the world” (v. 7), and the “for” most naturally ties the warning to the command. Love is not a soft subject to cover before the serious one; it is part of the church’s defense. The deceivers had “gone out” from the fellowship (1 John 2:19), and error tends to take root where love has already cooled. A church whose members are knit together in obedient love is very hard to split, while a church full of grievances is easy to enter. The more love shapes believers, the better they recognize and resist false teachers. Before a church sharpens its arguments, it should strengthen its love. Has our love for the believers around us cooled in ways that leave our fellowship open to division and deception?
items.q: Has our love for the believers around us cooled in ways that leave our fellowship open to division and deception?

items.title: Christ Walked the Road He Calls Us To (2 John 1:6–7)
items.html: John’s command to walk according to Christ’s commandments has a living model in Christ Himself. Jesus never set truth aside to seem kind, because abandoning truth would not have been kindness, and He never used truth as license for pride or harshness. He sought what was truly good for people even when it cost Him their approval, confronting hypocrisy as readily as He welcomed sinners to His table. The walk this letter asks of its readers, truth and love refusing to separate, is simply the shape of Jesus’ own life, held out to His people as the road home.
items.q: John’s command to walk according to Christ’s commandments has a living model in Christ Himself.

sections.title: Abide in the Doctrine of Christ
Do Not Receive the Teacher Who Denies Christ

items.title: Two Comings at the Door (2 John 1:7, 10)
items.html: The same verb stands at the center of both warnings. In verse 7 the issue is Jesus Christ “coming” in the flesh; in verse 10 it is anyone who “comes” to your house. The One who came all the way to us in a body is the measure of everyone else who comes to us in His name. The deceiver comes to the door with a Christ who never really came, a spiritual idea instead of the Word made flesh. The question at every door, pulpit, podcast, and bookshelf is the same: does the one who comes confess the One who came? God crossed the whole distance to dwell with us in flesh, and He will not have His people welcome a message that sends Him back into the clouds.
items.q: The same verb stands at the center of both warnings.

items.title: The Assault on the Flesh of Christ (2 John 1:7–11)
items.html: Read as a whole, this section shows why John is so fiercely protective. The section moves from naming the enemy (v. 7), to an inward warning (v. 8), to the anatomy of departure (v. 9), to a quarantine (v. 10), to the cost of breaching it (v. 11). The deceivers were not making a minor theological error; they were attacking the very bridge between heaven and earth, the flesh of Jesus. The Gnostic idea was that spirit is entirely good and matter entirely evil, so God could never touch a body. John insists that God invaded the material world. If Christ did not come in the flesh, humanity cannot be redeemed. The antichrist spirit always seeks to disembody faith, to make it a purely intellectual or mystical exercise, divorced from how we treat human bodies, how we live in the physical world, and how God stooped to material reality. A disembodied faith asks for no physical obedience and no sacrifice. That is exactly its appeal, and exactly its lie.
items.q: Read as a whole, this section shows why John is so fiercely protective.

items.title: The Dark Koinonia (2 John 1:10–11)
items.html: We usually associate fellowship with the communion of the saints. But this section reveals a terrifying counterpart: fellowship with darkness by proxy. Merely by platforming, funding, or formally wishing success to a purveyor of false doctrine, a believer enters into a spiritual partnership with the fruit of that teacher’s ministry. The same word that describes our fellowship with the Father and the Son can describe a partnership with evil.
items.q: We usually associate fellowship with the communion of the saints.

items.title: The Harsh Edge of Perfect Love (2 John 1:7–11)
items.html: Modern definitions of love treat exclusion as the ultimate sin. John shatters that paradigm. Because he loves the church, he commands it to firmly exclude deceivers. True love builds walls around the sheepfold; to welcome a wolf is to hate the sheep. Strict doctrinal boundaries feel unloving to modern sensibilities, yet here a firm border against those who deny Christ is an act of motherly and fatherly care. A shepherd who will not fence the pasture does not truly love the sheep. Spiritual hospitality must be governed by truth, and when hospitality threatens the truth, it ceases to be a virtue. Shepherding a flock takes the courage to set hard boundaries, and believers need to learn that true love for the sheep sometimes requires holy intolerance for the wolves.
items.q: Modern definitions of love treat exclusion as the ultimate sin.

items.title: What a Welcome Really Carries (2 John 1:10–11)
items.html: Receiving a traveling teacher into a first-century home did more than offer a bed; it supplied him lodging, resources, credibility, and access to other believers who would hear him next. That is why John’s instruction is stern: welcoming such a man did not stay private; it helped a false message about Christ keep moving. The warning carries its own boundary. It is not permission for guilt by association or for cutting off every believer who disagrees with us; it targets the specific act of lending meaningful support to someone actively spreading a lie about who Jesus is.
items.q: Receiving a traveling teacher into a first-century home did more than offer a bed; it supplied him lodging, resources, credibility, and access to other believers who would hear him next.

items.title: Love Does Not Call Sin Good (2 John 1:10–11)
items.html: John’s warning concerns false teachers, but it rests on a principle that reaches further: truth and love cannot be separated, so love cannot celebrate what God calls sin. Paul says the same thing from the other direction: love “does not rejoice in iniquity, but rejoices in the truth” (1 Corinthians 13:6). This is not permission to withdraw from people whose lives do not match Scripture; Jesus welcomed sinners, ate with them, and moved toward the very people others avoided. It does mean that welcoming someone and affirming everything in that person’s life are not the same thing, a distinction that grows costly when the person is someone we love. Is there someone we love who wants us to celebrate something Scripture calls sin? Can we answer with both humility and faithfulness, without choosing between loving them and loving the truth?
items.q: Can we answer with both humility and faithfulness, without choosing between loving them and loving the truth?

sections.title: Hope of Speaking Face to Face

items.title: Joy at the Beginning, Joy at the End, and a “Rejoice!” That Cannot Be Given Away (2 John 1:4, 10–12)
items.html: The body of the letter is framed by joy. It opens with “I was very glad” (v. 4) over children walking in truth and closes with the hope “that your joy may be made full” (v. 12). In between, John forbids one word: the greeting chairein (vv. 10–11), which literally means “Rejoice!” The same word family runs through all three places. A believer cannot say “Rejoice!” over the work of someone who is tearing down the very truth that produces joy. Guarding the truth is guarding joy: the shut door of verse 10 protects the gladness of verse 4 and makes room for the full joy of verse 12. Joy in this letter is not a mood but the fruit of truth, love, and fellowship, and it is worth protecting.
items.q: The body of the letter is framed by joy.

items.title: The Joy-Completing Gathering (2 John 1:12–13)
items.html: The section moves from setting down the pen, to the hope of gathering, to joy made full, to a family greeting. In a world increasingly mediated by screens, text, and virtual presence, John’s closing words are an anchor. Paper and ink, the technology of his day, were not enough for the fullness of Christian experience. Individual joy can be profound, but there is a category of joy, a fullness, that remains out of reach in isolation. There is a joining of spirits and a completion of joy that happens only when believers gather face to face. The joy of the Lord reaches its high-water mark in the gathered, embodied assembly of the saints.
items.q: The section moves from setting down the pen, to the hope of gathering, to joy made full, to a family greeting.

items.title: From Paper and Ink to Face to Face: A Picture of the Covenants (2 John 1:12–13)
items.html: Read spiritually, John’s move from “paper and ink” to “face to face” traces the shape of redemptive history. The old covenant was written in ink and carved on stone; it communicated the truth but could not carry the fullness of joy (2 Corinthians 3:3). The new covenant is the Word made flesh, the face-to-face reality of Jesus Christ dwelling among us. John, speaking in the Spirit of Christ, longs to move the church from the written page to the living encounter.
items.q: Read spiritually, John’s move from “paper and ink” to “face to face” traces the shape of redemptive history.

items.title: Hoping to Speak Face to Face (2 John 1:12–13)
items.html: These closing verses are more than a sign-off. They carry the letter’s last themes, presence and joy made full, and they end not with a rule but with a hope: “I hope to come to you.” The God who came in the flesh has a people who long to come to one another.
items.q: These closing verses are more than a sign-off.

1.brief: The Elder, who does not give his name, writes to “the elect lady and her children,” most likely a local church chosen by God and its members, though the words could also describe a Christian woman and her family. He loves them “in truth,” and so do all who have known the truth, because the truth that joins believers to Christ also joins them to one another.
1.explain:
“The Elder,”

The writer gives no name, only a title. The Greek word for “elder” means an older man, and in the early church it also became the title of a church leader. Peter called himself “a fellow elder” (1 Peter 5:1). The first readers knew exactly who “the Elder” was, and the title alone carried the weight of a trusted leader writing to people he knew. The church has long identified him as John the apostle, and the letter’s language closely matches John’s Gospel and 1 John. Third John opens with the same title (3 John 1).

“To the elect lady and her children,”

“Elect” means chosen by God. The New Testament uses the word for believers whom God has called to belong to Himself, as when Peter writes to those who are “elect according to the foreknowledge of God the Father” (1 Peter 1:2). The Greek word for “lady” is the feminine form of the word for “lord,” a respectful way to address a woman.

The elect lady is most likely a local church, addressed as a woman, and “her children” are its members. The letter’s closing greeting from “the children of your elect sister” (verse 13) fits one congregation greeting another, and the way the Elder moves between addressing the lady and addressing a whole group of people supports the same reading. The words could also describe an individual Christian woman and her family. Either way, the Elder writes to people God has chosen and drawn into His family.

“whom I love in truth,”

The Elder’s love is genuine, not a polite formula at the head of a letter. It is also love grounded in the truth revealed in and about Jesus Christ. He does not love these believers because they are pleasant or because they treat him well. He loves them because the same truth of Christ has laid hold of him and of them, and that truth is the bond between them.

“and not only I, but also all those who have known the truth,”

This love is not the Elder’s alone. Everyone who has come to know the truth shares it. To have “known the truth” is more than having learned facts about Jesus. It is to have come to know the One who said, “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6), and to go on knowing Him. This congregation did not stand alone. Believers far beyond their city loved them, because the same truth had brought them all into one family.
1.notes:
The opening names neither the sender nor the recipient. The Elder has traditionally been identified as John the apostle.

The church historian Eusebius, writing in the fourth century, quoted the early bishop Papias, who listed John among the Lord’s disciples and then separately mentioned “the elder John.” Eusebius concluded that there were two Johns and suggested that the second was probably the one who saw the Revelation.

Some scholars follow Eusebius and assign 2 and 3 John to this elder. Others read Papias as speaking of the same John twice, once among the apostles and once as still living. The traditional identification remains well supported, but the question is debated.

The Greek phrase for “elect lady” is eklektē kyria. Some have taken one of these words as a personal name, either “the lady Electa” or “the elect Kyria.” Kyria is found as a woman’s name, though rarely and mostly in later sources. “Electa” faces a difficulty, because verse 13 calls the sister “elect” as well, so both sisters would bear the same name.

The grammar also bears on the question. The lady is addressed with a singular “you” in verses 4–5 and 13, but verses 6, 8, 10, and 12 use a plural “you,” as if a group of people were being addressed under one name.

reflections.title: The Elder Who No Longer Needed His Name
reflections.html: “The elder to the chosen lady and her children.” The word for elder (presbyteros) means “an older man,” and by the time this letter was written John was likely the last living apostle, an old man at Ephesus. This is the John whom Jesus nicknamed a “son of thunder” (Mark 3:17), who wanted to call fire down on a Samaritan village (Luke 9:54) and asked for the seat at Jesus’ right hand (Mark 10:37). Now he does not even sign his name, just as in his Gospel he never names himself but is “the disciple whom Jesus loved.” He writes with apostolic authority, but he carries it as pastoral, fatherly care. True spiritual authority in the later years of ministry rests less on titles and more on character, faithfulness over time, and the spiritual weight of having walked with God. Decades with Jesus had not made John larger in his own eyes; they had made him gentler and smaller. Authority that has been with Jesus long enough no longer needs a title to be heard. Have our years with Jesus made us gentler and smaller in our own eyes, or more eager for recognition?
reflections.q: Have our years with Jesus made us gentler and smaller in our own eyes, or more eager for recognition?

reflections.title: The Lord’s Lady
reflections.html: “To the chosen lady.” “Lady” (kyria) is the feminine form of kyrios, “Lord,” and occurs in the New Testament only here and in verse 5. Many interpreters have read her as a local church personified as a mother whose “children” are its members, with her “chosen sister” (v. 13) a sister congregation. If so, John has given the congregation the feminine of her Master’s title: she is the Lord’s lady, chosen before she ever chose Him. Whether she was a particular woman hosting a house church or a congregation, the spiritual reality is the same. The church is a chosen bride, dignified, royal, and entrusted with raising spiritual children. She is both singular, one “lady,” and corporate, a household of “children,” just as each believer is individually chosen and yet all together form one bride. Scripture’s story moves toward a chosen woman made ready for her Lord (Ephesians 5:25–27; Revelation 19:7; 21:9). When we encounter Jesus deeply, He awakens in us a deep affection for His church; we cannot love the Bridegroom without loving His bride. A church is not an organization Christ manages; she is a bride He chose and loves. Do we speak of the church as something we attend, or as a bride Christ chose?
reflections.q: Do we speak of the church as something we attend, or as a bride Christ chose?

reflections.title: The Perimeter of Christian Love
reflections.html: “Whom I love in the truth.” John immediately defines the boundaries of his affection. Christian love is not a vague, borderless sentimentality; biblical love is never blind. It is rooted, bounded, and energized by eternal truth. “In truth” can also mean “truly, really”: John’s love is genuine because it stands on what is real. We cannot genuinely love fellow believers outside the context of the truth we share.
reflections.q: “Whom I love in the truth.”

reflections.title: Loving From the Indwelling Life
reflections.html: In John’s writings “the truth” is not finally a set of doctrines but a Person, Jesus Christ (John 14:6). So to love “in the truth” is to love from the shared, indwelling life of Christ Himself. That moves our fellowship out of mere human sympathy and into eternal, divine reality. Believers do not merely like one another; the life of Christ in one recognizes and loves the life of Christ in the other.
reflections.q: In John’s writings “the truth” is not finally a set of doctrines but a Person, Jesus Christ (John 14:6).

reflections.title: The Invisible Network of the Truth
reflections.html: “And not I only, but also all who know the truth.” The phrase means those who came to know the truth and still know it. Truth here is not a sterile set of facts but a living ecosystem that produces love among all who live in it. It creates an immediate, unbreakable, invisible network of fellowship among strangers. If you know the truth, you are bound in affection to everyone else who knows it, though you have never met.
reflections.q: “And not I only, but also all who know the truth.”

reflections.title: A Lady Without a Name
reflections.html: Interpreters have read “the chosen lady” as a woman named Kyria, an unnamed Christian mother and her household, or a local church. The plural “you” in verses 6, 8, 10, and 12 favors a church. John may have withheld names because of persecution. Whatever her identity, the letter treats her the way God treats His people: by her calling, not her fame.
reflections.q: Interpreters have read “the chosen lady” as a woman named Kyria, an unnamed Christian mother and her household, or a local church.

2.brief: The Elder gives the reason for this shared love: “the truth which abides in us and will be with us forever.” The truth revealed in Jesus Christ has made its home in believers and will never leave them, and that living, lasting truth is the ground of their love for one another.
2.explain:
“because of the truth”

The Elder now gives the reason for the shared love of verse 1. It rests on “the truth.” In John’s writings truth is more than accurate information. It is the reality God has made known in Jesus Christ. The Word who became flesh was “full of grace and truth” (John 1:14), and Jesus said of Himself, “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6). The truth the Elder speaks of is the apostolic message about Jesus, and it cannot be separated from Jesus Himself.

That is why believers who had never met could love one another. Their bond did not depend on shared background, personality, or local friendship. It rested on the same Lord and the same truth about Him.

“which abides in us”

The Greek word translated “abides” means to remain, to stay, or to make one’s home. It is one of John’s favorite words. Jesus used it when He said, “Abide in Me, and I in you” (John 15:4). The truth has come to live in believers, and it goes on living in them. The words closely parallel Jesus’ promise of another Helper, “that He may abide with you forever,” whom He called “the Spirit of truth” (John 14:16–17). The Elder does not name the Spirit here, but the parallel helps the reader see that the truth of Christ is not a lifeless idea stored in the mind. It dwells in God’s people.

The Elder says “us,” including himself with the believers he writes to. The same truth lives in him and in members of a church far from where he is, and that is what makes them one family.

“and will be with us forever:”

The truth that lives in believers is not temporary. Opinions change and teachers come and go, but “the word of our God stands forever” (Isaiah 40:8). John drew the same contrast in his first letter: “the world is passing away, and the lust of it; but he who does the will of God abides forever” (1 John 2:17). Because the truth will be with believers forever, the love that grows from it rests on something that will never pass away.

reflections.title: The Truth Moved In to Stay
reflections.html: “For the sake of the truth which abides in us and will be with us forever.” The verb menō means to remain, to stay, to make one’s home; the truth is not a visitor in the believer but a resident. As one old preacher said, we entertain it not as a guest but as the master of the house. John’s wording echoes Jesus’ promise in the upper room about the Spirit of truth: “that He may abide with you forever … He dwells with you and will be in you” (John 14:16–17). So the truth in this verse speaks with the voice of a Person. It has agency: it lives, it abides, it lasts forever. It is Christ, who is the truth (John 14:6), the living, risen Christ making His home in our hearts by the Spirit of truth, the uncreated life of God at work in a human vessel. We do not merely hold the truth; the Truth holds us. Two prepositions carry the promise: the truth abides in us and will be with us, life within and company alongside. What we hold as doctrine is the presence of Someone who has promised never to leave. Is the truth a guest in our lives, welcome when convenient, or the master of the house?
reflections.q: Is the truth a guest in our lives, welcome when convenient, or the master of the house?

reflections.title: The Permanence of the Indwelling
reflections.html: “And will be with us forever,” literally, “into the age,” with “with us” in the emphatic position. In a world of shifting philosophies and fading empires, the truth God has planted in His people is no passing philosophy but a permanent fixture. What God establishes within the human spirit outlasts time itself, and that permanence is the security of the saint.
reflections.q: “And will be with us forever,” literally, “into the age,” with “with us” in the emphatic position.

3.brief: The greeting becomes a confident promise: grace, mercy, and peace “will be with you” from God the Father and from “the Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of the Father.” These gifts come from the Father and the Son together, and they come “in truth and love,” the two words the rest of the letter will develop.
3.explain:
“Grace, mercy, and peace”

Grace is God’s kindness given freely to people who have not earned it. Mercy is His compassion toward the guilty and helpless, meeting them in their need instead of giving them what they deserve. Peace carries the fullness of the Hebrew idea of shalom: not only the end of hostility with God but the wholeness and well-being that come from being right with Him. Grace is the source, mercy is that grace reaching people in their need, and peace is what it produces in their lives. Paul uses the same three words when he greets Timothy (1 Timothy 1:2; 2 Timothy 1:2).

“will be with you”

Most New Testament letters open with a prayer that grace and peace would be given. The Elder speaks with confidence instead. These blessings “will be with you.” He is not hoping God might be kind to these believers; he is assuring them that God’s grace, mercy, and peace will remain with those who belong to the truth. That assurance matters in a letter that will soon warn about deceivers. The church’s security rests on what God will surely give.

“from God the Father and from the Lord Jesus Christ,”

Only God can give grace and mercy, and the Elder names two sources, the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. Repeating the word “from” places Jesus beside the Father as the giver of these blessings, not merely the channel through which they pass. That is fitting only because Jesus is Himself God. As John’s Gospel opens, “the Word was God” (John 1:1).

“the Son of the Father,”

In the NKJV this exact phrase appears only here. The Elder could have stopped with the name “the Lord Jesus Christ,” but he adds this description to stress the relationship between Jesus and the Father. Jesus is not a lesser messenger sent from God. He is the Father’s own Son, and through Him the Father is made known (John 1:18; 14:9). This careful wording prepares for the danger the Elder will soon address, teachers who deny the truth about Jesus Christ, when in fact the Son and the Father cannot be separated (verse 9).

“in truth and love.”

Grace, mercy, and peace are received within the truth revealed in and about Jesus Christ, and they show themselves in love. The Elder joins the two words here, and the rest of the letter develops them: truth lived in love (verses 4–6) and truth guarded (verses 7–11). Truth and love are not rival values to be balanced against each other. Believers live out the truth about Christ by loving one another.

reflections.title: A Promise, Not a Wish
reflections.html: “Grace, mercy and peace will be with us.” Paul’s greetings usually have no verb (“Grace to you and peace”), and Peter and Jude pray that grace be “multiplied”; John uses a plain future: “will be.” The greeting is a statement of assurance, not a prayer. It repeats the words of verse 2: the truth “will be with us,” and grace, mercy and peace “will be with us.” John is not hoping God will be kind to this house; he is announcing that He will. The God who guarantees that His truth will stay also guarantees that His grace stays with it.
reflections.q: “Grace, mercy and peace will be with us.”

reflections.title: Grace Bends Down to Become Mercy
reflections.html: Grace, mercy, and peace stand together only here and in Paul’s letters to Timothy, and this is the only appearance of “mercy” anywhere in John’s writings. The order is deliberate. Grace is God’s free, unmerited love in His own heart, the fountain; it has no cause outside God, who loves because He is God. Mercy is that love stooping to human misery, stepping into our weakness, failure, and the consequences of sin, as grace answers our guilt. Peace, shalom, is what results in us: wholeness and restoration once grace and mercy have done their work. The order runs from the first motion of God to the final satisfaction of man. We cannot know His peace without first receiving His mercy, and His mercy is born entirely of His grace. The old apostle, writing to a church under threat, does not begin with the danger but with the downward flow of God’s goodness. Everything God asks of this church in the verses that follow rests on what He has already given.
reflections.q: Grace, mercy, and peace stand together only here and in Paul’s letters to Timothy, and this is the only appearance of “mercy” anywhere in John’s writings.

reflections.title: The Son of the Father
reflections.html: “From God the Father and from Jesus Christ, the Son of the Father.” The title “the Son of the Father” occurs nowhere else in Scripture. John repeats “from” before both names, so that grace flows from the Son as truly as from the Father, in full equality. In a letter written against teachers who split the man Jesus from the divine Christ, the greeting itself confesses that Jesus Christ is the Father’s own Son, striking at the error before John names it. The title also speaks of intimacy: He is the Son who belongs to the Father, and the warm relationship within the Godhead is what believers are invited into. Salvation is not a transaction with a distant deity but an invitation into the love between a Father and His Son, and grace comes to us from both.
reflections.q: “From God the Father and from Jesus Christ, the Son of the Father.”

reflections.title: The Twin Banks of the River of Blessing
reflections.html: Grace, mercy, and peace will be with us “in truth and love,” a pair that appears together nowhere else and sums up the letter. Truth and love act as the two banks of a river. Without both banks firmly in place, the waters of grace, mercy, and peace spread into a muddy swamp of compromise or dry into a rigid desert of legalism. To abandon either is to dam up the flow of God’s blessing. Lasting peace is impossible outside the boundaries of truth and love. Breathe the twin atmosphere of truth and love daily, for only there can we carry the grace and mercy of the Son to a broken generation.
reflections.q: Grace, mercy, and peace will be with us “in truth and love,” a pair that appears together nowhere else and sums up the letter.

reflections.title: Grace Is a Person, Not a Package
reflections.html: Grace and peace are not abstract commodities we “get” from God. They are realized only as we possess the Person of Christ as our very life, and as we experience the Father’s deep affection for us. The blessing comes “from” Father and Son because it comes in Them.
reflections.q: Grace and peace are not abstract commodities we “get” from God.

4.brief: The Elder rejoices greatly that he has found some of the lady’s children “walking in truth,” living day by day in line with what God has revealed, just as the Father commanded. He speaks of those he has met; his words do not imply that the others had turned away.
4.explain:
“I rejoiced greatly”

The body of the letter begins with joy. The Elder uses the same words in 3 John: “For I rejoiced greatly when brethren came and testified of the truth that is in you, just as you walk in the truth” (3 John 3), and he adds, “I have no greater joy than to hear that my children walk in truth” (3 John 4). Nothing gladdened him more than believers who stayed faithful. His joy also shows his heart toward this church. He writes as one who loves them, not as a distant critic, and the warnings that follow come from that same love.

“that I have found some of your children”

The “children” are the members of the church addressed as the lady. The Elder does not say how he “found” them. He may have met some of them as they traveled or received reports about them, but the letter does not explain. “Some” refers to those he had come to know. It does not imply that the rest had turned away. Still, the warnings that follow show that the church faced real danger, so news that some members were standing firm was especially welcome.

“walking in truth,”

In Scripture, “walking” describes a person’s whole way of life, how he conducts himself day by day. “Enoch walked with God” (Genesis 5:24), and the psalmist prayed, “Teach me Your way, O LORD; I will walk in Your truth” (Psalm 86:11). John uses the word the same way: whoever says he abides in Christ “ought himself also to walk just as He walked” (1 John 2:6). The Greek form describes something ongoing. These believers were steadily living this way, not doing so only now and then.

To walk in truth is to live in line with the truth revealed in and about Jesus Christ. It includes believing that truth, but it reaches into daily conduct, so that what believers confess about Jesus is visible in how they live. That is what gave the Elder such joy.

“as we received commandment from the Father.”

Walking in truth is not a way of life believers invent for themselves. It is obedience to what the Father has commanded. “We” places the Elder alongside his readers under the same command from the same Father. John states that command plainly in his first letter: “And this is His commandment: that we should believe on the name of His Son Jesus Christ and love one another, as He gave us commandment” (1 John 3:23). Believing the truth about the Son and loving one another belong to one command, which the next two verses take up.

reflections.title: What Makes an Old Apostle Very Glad
reflections.html: “I was very glad to find some of your children walking in truth.” The word “very” appears in John’s writings only here and in 3 John 3, both times about believers walking in the truth. “I have found” is the same verb Andrew used when he ran to Simon with “We have found the Messiah” (John 1:41). An apostle who had seen the risen Christ, outlived his friends, and watched churches divide finds his greatest gladness in meeting the children of this house living what they believe (3 John 4). For the pastor, the discipler, or the parent, there is no greater joy than seeing the next generation not only affirming doctrine but ordering their daily lives by it, the seed of the gospel turning into holy living. The joy of finding Christ is completed in the joy of finding others walking with Him. Pastors and parents still know no greater gladness. Whose walk with God brings us joy, and have we told them?
reflections.q: Whose walk with God brings us joy, and have we told them?

reflections.title: Rejoice Over the Some
reflections.html: “Some of your children” means “some from among.” Perhaps John was too courteous to mention those who were not walking in truth; good parents do not always have good children, as Cain, Ishmael, and Esau remind us; or perhaps he simply reports the ones he met. Either way, he does not pretend everyone is perfectly aligned with God, and he does not let the “some” he has not seen silence his joy over the “some” he has. Many godly parents and pastors carry an ache for those who have wandered and lose the gladness God offers in those who are walking. Draw deep joy from the faithful ones and the real growth you can see. Thank God for the walkers by name, and keep praying for the rest from a heart that is still glad. Has grief over those who are not walking stolen our gladness over those who are?
reflections.q: Has grief over those who are not walking stolen our gladness over those who are?

reflections.title: Truth Is a Road, Not a Chair
reflections.html: “Walking in truth.” “Walk” describes a settled way of life, the Jewish idiom for daily conduct and habitual behavior (1 John 1:6–7; 2:6). Truth is not a chair to sit in; it is a path to walk on. It requires momentum, balance, and direction. A believer who has right doctrine but no righteous motion is not walking in truth; walking means taking the doctrine out of the notebook and putting it into our shoes. It is much easier to study the truth, or even argue about it, than to practice it. And walking is not taking a step or two; it is a whole way of going. A faith that does not command our feet has not truly conquered our hearts. Where has God’s truth actually begun to govern how we live, and where do we only agree with it from a safe distance?
reflections.q: Where has God’s truth actually begun to govern how we live, and where do we only agree with it from a safe distance?

reflections.title: The Normal Christian Walk
reflections.html: Spiritual reality is proven in the ordinary steps of obedience. This “normal Christian walk” is simply the outward, natural expression of the inward, living Christ having His way in us. Walking in truth is not our performance for Him but His life moving through us.
reflections.q: Spiritual reality is proven in the ordinary steps of obedience.

reflections.title: Walking by a Father’s Word
reflections.html: “Just as we have received commandment from the Father.” Walking in truth is not merely a philosophy; it is obedience to a Father’s word, a command received “from alongside the Father.” The road has an Author, and He is our Father.
reflections.q: “Just as we have received commandment from the Father.”

5.brief: With personal warmth the Elder pleads with the lady, not to introduce a new commandment but to renew the one they have had “from the beginning”: “that we love one another.” This is Jesus’ own command, heard when their life in Christ began, and by saying “we” the Elder places himself under it as well.
5.explain:
“And now I plead with you, lady,”

The Elder turns from his joy over the faithful children to a personal appeal. The Greek word translated “plead” usually means to ask or request. He could simply have given orders. Instead he speaks as one who loves this church and wants its members to respond willingly. The appeal is addressed to the “lady,” and through her it reaches all her children together.

“not as though I wrote a new commandment to you,”

The Elder is not adding anything to what they already believe. John made the same point in his first letter: “Brethren, I write no new commandment to you, but an old commandment which you have had from the beginning” (1 John 2:7). The command had been new when Jesus gave it on the night before His death: “A new commandment I give to you, that you love one another; as I have loved you, that you also love one another” (John 13:34). It was new because Jesus’ own love set its measure. By the time of this letter it had been part of Christian life for decades. It is old because it has always belonged to the faith, not because it has stopped mattering.

“but that which we have had from the beginning:”

“From the beginning” points back to the time these believers first received the gospel. Love for one another was not added to the message later. It was there from the start: “For this is the message that you heard from the beginning, that we should love one another” (1 John 3:11). The Elder says “we,” not “you,” placing himself under the same command as the newest believer.

This matters because others were coming with a message that departed from what believers first received (verse 7). The Elder does not ask his readers to move on to something fresh. He asks them to hold on to what they already have.

“that we love one another.”

This is love within the family of believers. Jesus made it the mark of His followers: “By this all will know that you are My disciples, if you have love for one another” (John 13:35). John shows what it looks like: “By this we know love, because He laid down His life for us. And we also ought to lay down our lives for the brethren” (1 John 3:16). It is more than warm feeling or kind words, for John also wrote, “let us not love in word or in tongue, but in deed and in truth” (1 John 3:18).

The Elder has just rejoiced over children walking in truth (verse 4), and now he places love beside that faithfulness. A church that holds firmly to the truth about Jesus must also love one another, because loving one another was part of that truth from the start. A familiar command can still be neglected, so he pleads with them to keep practicing it.

reflections.title: The Same Sermon an Old Man Kept Preaching
reflections.html: “Not as though I were writing to you a new commandment, but the one which we have had from the beginning, that we love one another.” An ancient tradition records that when John at Ephesus was so old that his disciples could scarcely carry him into the assembly, he would say at each meeting only, “Little children, love one another.” When they grew tired of hearing it and asked why he always said this, he answered, “It is the commandment of the Lord, and if this only be done, it is enough.” In this verse we hear the same old man saying the same thing in ink. The church rarely needs a new commandment as much as it needs to keep the one it was given, and the voice that keeps repeating it may be the most loving voice in the room.
reflections.q: “Not as though I were writing to you a new commandment, but the one which we have had from the beginning, that we love one another.”

reflections.title: An Apostle Who Asks
reflections.html: “Now I ask you, lady.” John had the right to command, yet he uses the verb “ask, request,” the very verb Jesus used for His own requests to the Father in the upper room: “I ask on their behalf” (John 17:9, 15, 20). He pleads rather than demands; true love cannot be legislated with a heavy hand; it must be requested and entered into willingly. Love will succeed where authority will not, and often the more authority is pressed, the more it is ignored. John also places himself under the command he gives: not “that you love one another,” but “that we love one another.” Leaders who ask, and who stand under the same word they preach, reach hearts that orders never touch. Is there someone we are trying to change by authority whom God is asking us to approach with a humble request?
reflections.q: Is there someone we are trying to change by authority whom God is asking us to approach with a humble request?

reflections.title: The Ancient Newness of the Command
reflections.html: John says this is not a new command, yet in 1 John 2:8 he calls it a new one. The command to love is as old as the nature of God Himself, rooted already in the Law (Leviticus 19:18), and it was “from the beginning” of their Christian lives. Yet it is new in kind, because it was perfectly lived out in the incarnation of Jesus (John 13:34) and must be freshly kindled by the Spirit in every generation. Spiritual maturity does not require novel doctrines; the profoundest realities of the faith are ancient. The enemy uses the craving for newness to distract believers from the hard, daily practice of the oldest command: love the brethren.
reflections.q: John says this is not a new command, yet in 1 John 2:8 he calls it a new one.

reflections.title: Love Is an Act of the Will
reflections.html: Love here is a commandment. That means agape love is fundamentally an act of the will, an obedience of the hands and feet, whatever the shifting temperature of our emotions. It has been called “undefeatable goodwill.” Love is the badge of the true Christian and the test of genuine faith. And it is hard to fake: belief may be feigned and confession may be only of the lips, but love is much harder to counterfeit.
reflections.q: Love here is a commandment.

reflections.title: Love Flows Like Sap in the Vine
reflections.html: We cannot manufacture this love. It must flow out of the divine life within, like sap in the vine (John 15:5). We can only give what we have received, so we position ourselves to encounter the Father’s love, and then pour it out on one another. “Love, and do what you will,” said Augustine, knowing that true divine love will fulfill the righteous requirements of God. This is not a burdensome code but the liberating law of love that governs the kingdom.
reflections.q: We cannot manufacture this love.

6.brief: The Elder now defines the love he has pleaded for: “This is love, that we walk according to His commandments.” Love for God and for one another shows itself in obedience to what God has said, and the commandment they have heard from the beginning is that they keep walking in that love.
6.explain:
“This is love, that we walk according to His commandments.”

In verse 5 the Elder asked the church to love one another. Here he says what that love is. To “walk” is to conduct one’s life, and the word points to a steady way of living rather than an occasional act. Love is seen in a life lived the way God has told His people to live. “His commandments” are the Father’s, since verse 4 spoke of the commandment received “from the Father,” and again the Elder includes himself in “we.”

Jesus taught His disciples the same thing: “If you love Me, keep My commandments” (John 14:15). John repeats it: “For this is the love of God, that we keep His commandments. And His commandments are not burdensome” (1 John 5:3). Love does not shrink to rule-keeping, because it flows from relationship with God, yet it cannot be separated from obeying Him. In verse 4 the faithful were “walking in truth”; here the same walk is described as walking “according to His commandments.” The life that holds to the truth is the life that loves, and both are seen in obedience.

“This is the commandment, that as you have heard from the beginning, you should walk in it.”

The Elder moves from many “commandments” to one “commandment.” All of God’s instructions come together in a single call. “As you have heard from the beginning” means since they first received the faith, so once more he is calling them to keep living by what they were first taught. “Walk in it” most naturally means walk in love, though the wording could point back to the commandment itself. The meaning is the same either way, because the Elder has bound the two together so tightly. Love is shown by keeping God’s commandments, and the commandment is to live a life of love.

reflections.title: Love Walks, and the Walk Is Love
reflections.html: “And this is love, that we walk according to His commandments. This is the commandment, just as you have heard from the beginning, that you should walk in it.” John defines love as obedience and then defines the commandment as love, a deliberate circle (John 14:15, 21; 1 John 5:3). Love produces obedience, and obedience proves love; they are the same substance seen from two angles. Love that does not obey is sentiment, emotional humanism; obedience that does not love is sterile legalism, law without the Lawgiver’s heart. The circle keeps each one honest. Our culture defines love as validation; John defines it as obedience to God. Love is an action, a matter of the will, not merely a feeling, and God’s commands are the safe, life-giving boundaries within which it can flourish. The circle also contradicted the false teachers’ claim to a purely intellectual enlightenment that asked nothing of how they lived. Love is best shown by obedience. We do not measure our love for God by how strongly we feel toward Him but by walking where His word leads, and no one walks that road long without learning to love. Where does our love for God stay in our feelings and never reach our feet?
reflections.q: Where does our love for God stay in our feelings and never reach our feet?

reflections.title: Love That Says No Is Still Love
reflections.html: John defines love by obedience rather than by feeling, and obedience does not always look like comfort. Love gives, forgives, and bears with another person, but it also corrects, sets a boundary, or speaks a hard truth when that is what genuinely helps someone. The test is never simply whether something feels loving, but whether it seeks what is truly good for the other person, as God has defined good, not as the moment defines it. A culture that measures love mainly by affirmation and avoided conflict will misread some of love’s most faithful acts as its opposite.
reflections.q: John defines love by obedience rather than by feeling, and obedience does not always look like comfort.

reflections.title: The Indwelling Christ Fulfills the Command
reflections.html: Here is the mystery of the gospel: the indwelling Christ fulfills the law in and through us when we yield to Him. True spiritual love is a fierce, unrelenting obedience to the highest authority, the Lord Jesus Himself, and yet it is not religious drudgery. It is a passionate, joyful pursuit of the Bridegroom’s will in everyday life.
reflections.q: Here is the mystery of the gospel: the indwelling Christ fulfills the law in and through us when we yield to Him.

7.brief: The opening “For” ties the warning to the call to love, because many deceivers have gone out into the world who do not confess Jesus Christ as coming in the flesh. To deny that the Son of God truly became human strikes at the heart of the faith, and the Elder calls the one who teaches it “a deceiver and an antichrist.”
7.explain:
“For many deceivers have gone out into the world”

The opening “For” links this warning to verses 4–6. The Elder has called the church to keep walking in the commandment they heard from the beginning, because there were people actively trying to lead them away from it. The Greek word for “deceivers” describes those who lead others astray, causing them to wander from the right path. They were not merely mistaken. They were spreading their error and drawing others after them.

Jesus had warned that “many false prophets will rise up and deceive many” (Matthew 24:11), and John uses almost the same words in his first letter: “many false prophets have gone out into the world” (1 John 4:1). “Have gone out” may also recall those of whom John wrote, “They went out from us, but they were not of us” (1 John 2:19). The Elder does not name these teachers or describe their whole system, and their identity is not known. What marks them is the denial he names next.

“who do not confess Jesus Christ as coming in the flesh.”

To “confess” is to acknowledge openly what is true. These deceivers would not acknowledge that Jesus Christ came as a real human being. “Flesh” here means a genuine human body and a real human life. John’s Gospel declares, “And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14), and 1 John begins with what the apostles had heard, seen, and handled with their own hands (1 John 1:1). Jesus was not a spirit who only seemed human.

This was no minor disagreement. The eternal Son of God took on real flesh and blood so that He could die for sinners. Because God’s children share in flesh and blood, Jesus “Himself likewise shared in the same, that through death He might destroy him who had the power of death, that is, the devil” (Hebrews 2:14). If Jesus did not truly become human, He did not truly die, and His blood did not truly pay for sin. John gives the same test in his first letter: “every spirit that does not confess that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is not of God” (1 John 4:3).

“This is a deceiver and an antichrist.”

The Elder moves from “many deceivers” to “this,” meaning that anyone who teaches this denial fits the description. He gives two names. A “deceiver” leads people away from the truth. An “antichrist” stands against Christ and puts something false in His place. In the New Testament the word appears only in John’s letters. The believers had heard “that the Antichrist is coming,” and John told them, “even now many antichrists have come” (1 John 2:18). The spirit of the Antichrist “is now already in the world” (1 John 4:3). The Elder does not say that each of these teachers is the coming Antichrist. He means that their teaching already carries the same opposition to Christ. To deny who Jesus truly is, however religious the teacher may sound, is to work against Christ Himself.
7.notes:
The wording here differs from the parallel test in 1 John 4:2. There the Greek wording, “has come in the flesh,” describes a completed event with lasting results. Here the wording literally means “Jesus Christ coming in flesh.”

A few interpreters have taken the present tense as a reference to Christ’s future return in bodily form. This Greek verb form can, however, describe who someone is rather than when an action happens, as in the question put to Jesus, “Are You the Coming One, or do we look for another?” (Matthew 11:3). The close link with 1 John 4:2 makes the incarnation the most natural meaning, though the present tense alone does not settle the question.

Who these teachers were is uncertain. Later writers describe teachings that would fit the Elder’s warning. One held that Christ only seemed to have a body, a view later called Docetism, from the Greek word for “to seem.” Another was attributed to Cerinthus, who, according to Irenaeus, taught that a divine Christ came upon the man Jesus after His baptism and left Him before the crucifixion. Either view would deny what the Elder insists on, but the letter gives too little detail to tie the deceivers to any known group.

reflections.title: Wanderers Make Wanderers
reflections.html: “For many deceivers have gone out into the world.” The word for deceiver belongs to the Greek family for wandering and leading astray; the “wandering stars” of Jude 13 are planētai, the source of our word “planet.” A deceiver is first a wanderer and then one who gathers others to wander with him, one who causes others to wander; such people are “deceiving and being deceived” (2 Timothy 3:13). These teachers had “gone out,” the verb John used of those who “went out from us” (1 John 2:19); they had left the fellowship and were traveling the circuit of house churches. Error rarely stays home. The cure for a wandering heart is not more motion but abiding.
reflections.q: “For many deceivers have gone out into the world.”

reflections.title: Deception Is on the Move
reflections.html: Deception is not passive; it is a proactive, invasive force moving out into the world and looking for a way into the church. Believers must live with spiritual alertness, aware that the world system is constantly flooded with teaching that denies the incarnate Christ. (The KJV reads “entered into the world”; the better text reads “gone out.” Either way, they were moving, and they were coming.)
reflections.q: Deception is not passive; it is a proactive, invasive force moving out into the world and looking for a way into the church.

reflections.title: A Bridge Broken at the Nearer End
reflections.html: “Those who do not acknowledge Jesus Christ as coming in the flesh.” Some taught that Jesus only seemed to have a body (Docetism, from the Greek for “to seem”); Cerinthus taught that the divine Christ came on the man Jesus at His baptism and left Him before the cross. Behind both lay the idea that spirit is good and flesh is evil. Either way, God never truly took on human flesh, never truly died, and never truly came near. “A Savior not quite God is a bridge broken at the farther end,” said one old bishop; the error John confronts breaks the bridge at the nearer end, a Savior not truly man. The whole story of Scripture is God coming to dwell with His people, and the incarnation is where He moved all the way in: “The Word became flesh, and dwelt among us” (John 1:14). To deny His flesh is to deny that God came to where we are.
reflections.q: “Those who do not acknowledge Jesus Christ as coming in the flesh.”

reflections.title: The Incarnational Test of Orthodoxy
reflections.html: The spirit of antichrist is identified by one refusal: it will not confess that Jesus came in the flesh. Why is the body of Jesus the ultimate battleground? Because if God did not take on real flesh, then the material world is simply evil, the physical cross was an illusion, the blood atonement never happened, bodily resurrection is a myth, and our own bodies cannot be temples of the Holy Spirit. The incarnation is the linchpin of redemption and the bedrock of our union with God: because Christ came in the flesh, He joined humanity to God. The identity of Jesus is the hill to die on. Get Jesus wrong, and you lose everything.
reflections.q: The spirit of antichrist is identified by one refusal: it will not confess that Jesus came in the flesh.

reflections.title: He Has Not Taken Off Our Flesh
reflections.html: In 1 John 4:2 the confession is that Jesus “has come” in the flesh; here John uses the present participle, “coming in the flesh.” Some take the present to describe the incarnation as an abiding fact rather than a finished event: Jesus came, and He continues in the flesh. Others refer it to His return; others warn against pressing the tense. Whatever the nuance, Scripture is clear that the risen Jesus did not lay aside His humanity. He ascended in a body of flesh and bones (Luke 24:39, 51); “there is one Mediator between God and men, the Man Christ Jesus” (1 Timothy 2:5); and He will return “in like manner” (Acts 1:11). A Man with scars sits at the Father’s right hand. The flesh He took for us He keeps for us.
reflections.q: In 1 John 4:2 the confession is that Jesus “has come” in the flesh; here John uses the present participle, “coming in the flesh.”

reflections.title: Against Christ, and Instead of Christ
reflections.html: “This is the deceiver and the antichrist.” Only John uses the word antichrist, and the prefix anti can mean “against” or “instead of”: the antichrist spirit opposes Christ by offering a substitute Christ. John is not calling each teacher the final Antichrist; he names the type. The spirit of antichrist is not only a future political figure but any present teaching that diminishes the glory and reality of the incarnate Son of God.
reflections.q: “This is the deceiver and the antichrist.”

reflections.title: The Son Who Came Near
reflections.html: John’s warning is anchored in a single fact: the Son of God truly took on flesh and entered the world He made. God did not send information about Himself from a safe distance; He came near, entered homes, touched people others avoided, wept with the grieving, and finally gave Himself on a cross. Guarding the truth about who Jesus is matters because it guards this very pattern. A church that defends the doctrine of the incarnation but never moves toward people the way the incarnate Christ did has kept the teaching and lost its shape.
reflections.q: John’s warning is anchored in a single fact: the Son of God truly took on flesh and entered the world He made.

reflections.title: Discernment Is Knowing the Real
reflections.html: Discernment is not suspicion of people; it is such intimate familiarity with the true Christ that the counterfeit is recognized at once.
reflections.q: Discernment is not suspicion of people; it is such intimate familiarity with the true Christ that the counterfeit is recognized at once.

8.brief: Because the danger is real, the Elder tells them, “Look to yourselves.” If they are drawn away, the fruit of the labor shared by the Elder and these believers could be lost, but his desire is that “we may receive a full reward,” though the verse does not define exactly what that reward or that loss will be.
8.explain:
“Look to yourselves,”

This is a call to be on guard. The command is plural, so the Elder is speaking to all the members of the church. Having just warned about deceivers (verse 7), he tells believers to keep watch over their own lives. Jesus gave a similar warning about false teachers: “Take heed that no one deceives you” (Matthew 24:4). Deceivers do their damage when believers stop paying attention, so the Elder does not tell them to study the false teachers more closely. He tells them to keep a careful eye on themselves.

“that we do not lose those things we worked for,”

The NKJV’s “we” includes the Elder with the believers he writes to. The word translated “worked” suggests real labor.
