What had been worked for was the fruit of the truth among these believers: their faith in Christ, their love for one another, and the walk in truth that gave the Elder such joy (verse 4). That fruit came through faithful teaching, prayer, and obedience, both theirs and their teachers’. Paul felt the same concern when the Galatians were being drawn away from the gospel: “I am afraid for you, lest I have labored for you in vain” (Galatians 4:11). If these believers welcomed teaching that denied who Jesus is, that labor could be lost.

“but that we may receive a full reward.”

A “reward” is what is paid for work done, and “full” means complete, with nothing missing. The danger of loss is real, and so is the prospect of receiving all that God intends to give. The Elder does not explain here how this reward relates to salvation or to persevering in faith, and Christians understand that relationship in different ways. His purpose is clear. He wants these believers to stay faithful to Christ so that nothing of what has been given and worked for is lost. John expressed the same concern in his first letter: “abide in Him, that when He appears, we may have confidence and not be ashamed before Him at His coming” (1 John 2:28).
8.notes:
The NKJV follows the majority of Greek manuscripts, which have “we” in all three clauses. Most modern translations follow a different Greek reading, with “you” in the first and last clauses and “we” in the middle, so that the readers are the ones who could lose or receive, and the labor at stake is what the Elder and other teachers had invested in them.

Other important manuscripts, including Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Alexandrinus, read “what you worked for” in the middle clause. On that reading the labor belongs to the readers themselves.

reflections.title: Guard the House From the Inside First
reflections.html: “Watch yourselves.” Before John tells the church what to do about the deceivers at the door (vv. 10–11), he tells them to look at themselves. The command is a present imperative: keep looking, keep watching. It is like securing your own fortress before going out to fight. Deceivers succeed less by their strength than by our unguarded places: pride, spiritual boredom, an itch for something new, the pull of deceptive cultural currents. The first defense against error is not suspicion of others but honest attention to our own hearts. Are we watching our own hearts, or only watching for error in other people?
reflections.q: Are we watching our own hearts, or only watching for error in other people?

reflections.title: Discernment That Starts With a Mirror
reflections.html: “Watch yourselves” is especially pointed in an age when exposing other believers’ errors can become an occupation of its own. Online ministries and churches alike can spend enormous energy cataloging other Christians’ theology, sermons, songs, and associations while giving little attention to their own hearts. John’s order matters: before the church is told what to do about the deceiver at the door, it is told to examine itself. Biblical watchfulness begins at home, with the honest question of where I am coasting or compromised, not with a list of everyone else’s faults.
reflections.q: “Watch yourselves” is especially pointed in an age when exposing other believers’ errors can become an occupation of its own.

reflections.title: God Wants to Pay in Full
reflections.html: “That you do not lose what we have accomplished, but that you may receive a full reward.” “Accomplished” means labored, and “reward” is a worker’s wage, the word for the laborers’ pay in the vineyard (Matthew 20:8) and the reaper’s wages in the harvest (John 4:36). John pictures a field that he and the church have worked together, now at risk of being lost just before payday; he wants them to hold on with him to the finish. The danger is not losing salvation but losing the fullness of what faithfulness would bring, the reward tested at the judgment seat of Christ (1 Corinthians 3:12–15). A “full” reward implies there can be a partial one: salvation is a free gift, but rewards are tied to our ongoing abiding, watchfulness, and faithful stewardship of the truth placed in us. Yet the God of this verse is not looking for reasons to withhold. He is a generous Master who wants to pay in full (Revelation 22:12), and ultimately He Himself is our “exceedingly great reward” (Genesis 15:1).
reflections.q: “That you do not lose what we have accomplished, but that you may receive a full reward.”

reflections.title: The Joint Venture of Spiritual Labor
reflections.html: “What we have accomplished.” John sees these believers’ growth as a shared investment; the apostle’s labor and their cooperation are woven together. If they fall to deception, part of his labor and joy is lost too. Spiritual progress can be lost: what apostles, pastors, and mentors have poured into us can be squandered by later carelessness. We are stewards not only of our own faith but of the labor others have invested in us. (The better text reads “that you do not lose what we have worked for, but that you may receive.”)
reflections.q: “What we have accomplished.”

reflections.title: Don’t Stumble Near the Finish Line
reflections.html: There is a tragedy in running the race well only to stumble near the end. Live for the smile of the Master rather than the comforts of the age, with the full reward of Christ’s presence as your highest motive. Our daily choices carry eternal weight; steward your spiritual momentum fiercely.
reflections.q: There is a tragedy in running the race well only to stumble near the end.

9.brief: Whoever “transgresses,” stepping beyond the teaching about Christ instead of remaining in it, “does not have God.” But the one who abides in the doctrine of Christ “has both the Father and the Son,” for remaining in the truth about Jesus cannot be separated from living fellowship with God through Christ Himself.
9.explain:
“Whoever transgresses”

To “transgress” is to step over a line or go beyond a boundary. The Elder has just described the deceivers (verse 7), and here he names what such a person does: he crosses the boundary of the truth about Christ and leaves it behind. Many modern translations read “goes ahead” or “runs ahead,” following a different Greek reading, but either way the person has moved past the teaching he first received instead of staying with it. “Whoever” makes the warning personal. It applies to anyone who takes this step, whether a visiting teacher or a church member drawn away.

“and does not abide in the doctrine of Christ”

“Abide” is the word used in verse 2, where the truth “abides in us.” Those in whom the truth lives must also go on living in it. “Doctrine” simply means teaching. “The doctrine of Christ” is the apostolic teaching about Jesus Christ, especially who He is and that He truly came in the flesh. John urged the same in his first letter: “Therefore let that abide in you which you heard from the beginning. If what you heard from the beginning abides in you, you also will abide in the Son and in the Father” (1 John 2:24).

Remaining in this teaching cannot be separated from remaining in Christ Himself. Jesus said, “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6), so the one who abandons the truth about who Jesus is has walked away from Jesus. Right words about Him are no substitute for knowing Him, yet no one can know Him while rejecting the truth about Him. The Elder’s concern is not a disagreement over secondary matters. It is the foundation itself, the identity of Jesus Christ and His coming in the flesh.

“does not have God.”

To “have” God is to know Him and belong to Him. Whatever a person may claim, if he leaves the truth about Christ behind, he does not have God. John said it just as plainly in his first letter: “Whoever denies the Son does not have the Father either” (1 John 2:23). No one reaches the Father by going around His Son.

“He who abides in the doctrine of Christ has both the Father and the Son.”

The one who stays with the teaching about Christ loses nothing. He has God, both “the Father and the Son.” The greeting called Jesus “the Son of the Father” (verse 3), and here that relationship bears fruit. The Father and the Son cannot be separated, for Jesus said, “He who does not honor the Son does not honor the Father who sent Him” (John 5:23). To hold to the truth about the Son is to enjoy fellowship with both. These believers did not need some new teaching to know God more deeply. Everything they needed was found in remaining with the Christ they had believed from the beginning.
9.notes:
Two different Greek words lie behind the translations of this verse. The NKJV’s “transgresses” translates parabainōn, the reading of most later manuscripts. Many modern translations read “goes ahead” or “runs ahead,” translating proagōn, found in several of the oldest manuscripts, including the fourth-century manuscripts known as Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus.

Elsewhere the Greek verb proagō is an ordinary word for going before or leading the way. Here it would describe moving forward past the teaching about Christ instead of remaining in it. Some interpreters suggest the word echoes the false teachers’ own claim to offer something more advanced. That is a reasonable guess, but the letter does not describe their claims.

“The doctrine of Christ” could grammatically mean the teaching Christ Himself gave or the teaching about Christ. The context favors teaching about Christ, since verse 7 has just named the denial of His coming in the flesh.

reflections.title: Running Ahead of the Teaching
reflections.html: “Anyone who goes too far and does not abide in the teaching of Christ does not have God.” The verb means “to go before, lead forward,” here in its bad sense: “goes on ahead,” “runs ahead,” “goes further than is right.” The false teachers claimed to be the progressives, the advanced thinkers, the men of the open and adventurous mind, possessors of a higher knowledge that had moved beyond the simple gospel of the apostles. John answers that progress beyond the foundational teaching of Christ is not enlightenment; it is abandonment. To leave the boundaries of Christ’s teaching is to leave God Himself. Progress that denies fundamental truth is going backward. Like a child who runs ahead of his father on a mountain trail, the one who outruns Christ’s teaching does not arrive sooner; he gets lost. Jesus Christ must be the touchstone of all thinking. The question to ask of any “new” teaching is not whether it is fresh but whether it is still inside Christ. Are we drawn to teaching because it sounds new or advanced?
reflections.q: Are we drawn to teaching because it sounds new or advanced?

reflections.title: The Prize of Sound Doctrine Is God Himself
reflections.html: “The one who abides in the teaching, he has both the Father and the Son.” To “have” God is John’s language for a real, living relationship: “He who has the Son has life” (1 John 5:12; 2:23). Abiding in the teaching means abiding in living union with the Person of Christ. The point is not to win arguments or guard a tradition but to possess the Father and the Son; when we remain in Christ, we receive not merely a teaching but the Father and the Son as our inward, abundant supply of life. Doctrine is the doorway, and the Father and the Son are the home it opens into. That is why John cares so much about what is taught concerning Jesus: a different Christ cannot bring anyone to the Father (John 14:6), and we cannot experience the true God through a false Jesus. We study the teaching so that through it we may have Him, and our study is not finished until we have entered. Is our knowledge of doctrine bringing us to have the Father and the Son, or only to have opinions about Them?
reflections.q: Is our knowledge of doctrine bringing us to have the Father and the Son, or only to have opinions about Them?

reflections.title: You Cannot Bypass the Son
reflections.html: There is no middle ground here between having God and being without Him. You cannot go around the Son to get to the Father. Any spirituality or religion that claims to possess the Father while altering or diminishing the Son is utterly bankrupt; a doctrine that diminishes Christ strips a person of a true relationship with the Father. Christ is the only place the Father is found. Don’t go on without Christ, or you will lose God.
reflections.q: There is no middle ground here between having God and being without Him.

10.brief: If anyone comes to them without this doctrine of Christ, they must not receive him into their house or greet him. The Elder has in view teachers who traveled from church to church and depended on believers’ welcome and support, so he forbids giving a Christ-denying ministry a home and a blessing, not ordinary kindness or conversation.
10.explain:
“If anyone comes to you”

The warning about deceivers who “have gone out into the world” (verse 7) now reaches the church’s own door. In the early church, teachers and missionaries traveled from town to town and depended on believers for lodging, meals, and help for the next stage of their journey. The Elder valued this hospitality. In 3 John he commends Gaius for receiving traveling brothers and urges sending them on “in a manner worthy of God” (3 John 6). The “you” here is plural, so the instruction concerns the whole congregation, not only one household.

“and does not bring this doctrine,”

“This doctrine” is the doctrine of Christ named in verse 9, the apostolic teaching about who Jesus Christ is, including His coming in the flesh. The word “bring” pictures a teacher arriving with a message he intends to spread. The church is not told to judge such a visitor by his gifts, his warmth, or his claims to insight. The deciding question is what he teaches about Jesus. The Elder has in mind someone who comes promoting a denial of the foundational truth about Christ, not a fellow believer who differs on lesser matters.

“do not receive him into your house”

Receiving a traveling teacher meant giving him a room, food, and supplies, and often a hearing among the believers. Churches commonly met in homes (Romans 16:5), so welcoming a teacher into the house may also have meant giving him a place to teach the gathered church, though the letter does not describe the setting in detail. That support made his work possible. In 3 John the Elder writes that believers should receive faithful workers “that we may become fellow workers for the truth” (3 John 8). The same principle works in reverse. Housing and supplying a Christ-denying teacher would make the church a partner in spreading his error.

The Elder is not forbidding help to a stranger in need, conversation with someone who holds wrong beliefs, ordinary hospitality, or loving relationships with family members and others who believe differently. He is forbidding the church to become a base of operations for someone working against the truth about Christ.

“nor greet him;”

The Greek word behind “greet” was the common word of greeting, related to the verb “rejoice.” The same word opens letters in the New Testament, where it is translated “Greetings” (Acts 15:23; James 1:1). For a visiting teacher, this greeting was more than a polite hello. It welcomed him as a fellow servant and wished his work well, showing him and the church that he came with their approval. That is the greeting the Elder tells them to withhold. Believers are not to treat such a person rudely. They are not to give a blessing that tells everyone his message has their support.
10.notes:
An early Christian manual called the Didache, probably written in the late first or early second century, shows how churches handled traveling teachers. It told believers to receive a teacher whose teaching agreed with what they had received, but not to listen to one who taught a different doctrine that undermined it.

It also gave practical tests. A traveling apostle was to stay one day, or two if necessary, and one who stayed three days, or who asked for money, was to be treated as a false prophet.

reflections.title: Your Door Is a Pulpit
reflections.html: “If anyone comes to you and does not bring this teaching, do not receive him into your house.” Church buildings did not appear until the third century; the church met in homes (Romans 16:5; Colossians 4:15; Philemon 2), and traveling teachers depended on believers to house and feed them while they taught. An early Christian manual, the Didache, instructs churches to receive a teacher who teaches these things, but not to listen to one who turns and teaches another doctrine, and it warns that a traveling teacher who stays three days or asks for money is a false prophet. To take such a man into the house was to give him a bed, a table, a gathered church, the host’s credibility, and a recommendation to the next town; refusing him lodging effectively shut down his ministry. Hospitality was the road the gospel traveled on (3 John 5–8), and the same road could carry poison. What we give a platform to, we help spread.
reflections.q: “If anyone comes to you and does not bring this teaching, do not receive him into your house.”

reflections.title: Check What He Brings
reflections.html: “And does not bring this teaching.” The test John gives is not the visitor’s warmth, gifting, eloquence, or credentials, but what he carries in. A teacher is a messenger, and messengers are judged by the message. Like a border guard who waves through a friendly traveler without checking the cargo, churches are often more impressed by the carrier than by what he brings. The Bereans checked the cargo against the Scriptures even when the carrier was Paul (Acts 17:11).
reflections.q: “And does not bring this teaching.”

reflections.title: Love That Is Fierce With Wolves
reflections.html: In the ancient world hospitality was a sacred duty, yet John commands a radical boundary. True love protects the flock, and refusing hospitality to wolves is an act of supreme love for the sheep. Love for the flock requires a shepherd to be fierce with the wolves; tolerance of a doctrine that denies the incarnation is not love but an abdication of protection. There is a holy intolerance for error that refuses to sacrifice truth on the altar of a false, superficial unity. Guard the sacred fire of your inner life, your home, and your church from false teaching, because toxic theology brings toxic spiritual realities. We are called to love all people, but we are forbidden to empower, endorse, or fund ministries that deny the biblical Jesus.
reflections.q: In the ancient world hospitality was a sacred duty, yet John commands a radical boundary.

reflections.title: Holy Severity, Rightly Bounded
reflections.html: The early church felt this severity. An old story tells that John, finding the false teacher Cerinthus in a bathhouse at Ephesus, rushed out, crying, “Let us flee, lest the bath fall, for Cerinthus, the enemy of the truth, is within.” Yet the command has edges. It has been called an emergency regulation, and emergency regulations can make bad law if stretched. It does not forbid ordinary courtesy, emergency help, or friendship, and it does not forbid speaking with someone at the door in order to reach him with the truth. It forbids receiving and endorsing a teacher who is actively spreading a false Christ.
reflections.q: The early church felt this severity.

11.brief: The reason follows: “he who greets him shares in his evil deeds.” To welcome and send such a teacher on with a blessing is to become a partner in spreading teaching that denies Christ, so the matter touches the church’s own faithfulness to Him.
11.explain:
“for he who greets him”

“For” gives the reason behind the command of verse 10. The greeting in view is the one that signals support, the kind of welcome that tells everyone this teacher is a trusted brother whose message deserves a hearing. The Elder is not forbidding ordinary courtesy toward someone who is wrong. He is saying that a believer should not lend his name, his home, or his encouragement to one who goes from church to church denying that Jesus Christ came in the flesh (verse 7).

“shares in his evil deeds.”

The Greek verb translated “shares” belongs to the same word family John uses for “fellowship” in his first letter: “truly our fellowship is with the Father and with His Son Jesus Christ” (1 John 1:3). To share in something is to become a partner in it. A believer who welcomes and supports a false teacher may not believe his error at all, but by opening the door he helps that teacher do his work and so takes part in it.

The “evil deeds” are not only private sins in the teacher’s life. They are the harm his teaching does as it leads people away from the truth about Jesus, causing them to lose what has been worked for (verse 8). Whoever leaves the doctrine of Christ “does not have God” (verse 9). Helping such a teacher therefore means helping to draw people away from the Father and the Son, which is why the Elder treats the matter so seriously.

The same principle runs the other way. In 3 John the Elder commends welcoming faithful traveling teachers, “that we may become fellow workers for the truth” (3 John 8). Support makes a person a partner in the message of the one he supports. Those who support a faithful teacher share in the work of the truth, and those who support a deceiver share in the damage he does.

reflections.title: A Greeting Can Be a Partnership
reflections.html: “For the one who gives him a greeting participates in his evil deeds.” “Participates” is the verb form of koinōnia, the word John used for “our fellowship … with the Father and with His Son Jesus Christ” (1 John 1:3). Fellowship is never neutral: the same kind of bond that joins us to God can, when misplaced, join us to another man’s evil work. False teaching is not just an unfortunate error; it is a wicked work, one that actively does harm. The greeting in view is not a polite hello on the street but a formal, public welcome that treats the teacher as a brother and his work as the Lord’s work; in that culture, hospitality and greeting conferred trust, patronage, and spiritual solidarity. We can become guilty of sins we did not physically commit. Financial, verbal, or social endorsement of a false ministry makes a believer a partner in the damage it does (1 Timothy 5:22). There is an unseen economy here: we are credited, for good or ill, with what we facilitate, fund, or formally endorse, and where we direct our support reveals the true alignment of our hearts. Loyalty to Christ must outrank cultural politeness. What are we giving a platform to, in our homes, our feeds, or our recommendations, that does not bring the truth about Jesus?
reflections.q: What are we giving a platform to, in our homes, our feeds, or our recommendations, that does not bring the truth about Jesus?

12.brief: The Elder has many more things to say but does not want to write them “with paper and ink.” He hopes instead to come and “speak face to face, that our joy may be full,” because the joy they share in Christ is made complete when they are together.
12.explain:
“Having many things to write to you,”

The letter is short, and the Elder admits there is much more he wants to say. He has written what was most urgent: the call to love one another, the warning about deceivers who deny that Jesus Christ came in the flesh, and the instruction not to receive and support them. The rest can wait. Third John closes in almost the same way (3 John 13–14).

“I did not wish to do so with paper and ink;”

The “paper” was papyrus, a writing sheet made from strips of a reed plant pressed together, and ink was commonly made from soot mixed with gum and water. The Elder is not saying that writing is wrong. He has just written this letter, and John’s Gospel was written “that you may believe” (John 20:31). But a letter has limits. It cannot answer questions, read a listener’s face, or give the warmth of being present. The Elder does not say why he chose to wait, only that he would rather speak in person.

“but I hope to come to you and speak face to face,”

The Greek expression behind “face to face” literally reads “mouth to mouth,” meaning direct, personal conversation with nothing in between. The Elder wanted to be with this church and its members, not merely to send them instructions from a distance. “I hope” shows that his plans were sincere but not certain. He longed to come, but whether and when he would arrive was not entirely in his hands.

“that our joy may be full.”

In verse 4 he “rejoiced greatly” over news of children walking in truth. That joy was real but not yet complete. Being together in person would bring it to its fullness. “Our” matters here. The joy belongs to the Elder and the believers together, because it comes from their shared life in the truth and in Christ.

John used nearly the same words at the start of his first letter: “And these things we write to you that your joy may be full” (1 John 1:4). He learned that language from Jesus, who said, “These things I have spoken to you, that My joy may remain in you, and that your joy may be full” (John 15:11). The full joy Jesus promised is found in fellowship with Him, and it overflows into fellowship among those who belong to Him. That is why the Elder wanted more than a letter could give.
12.notes: The closing of 3 John is strikingly similar. There the Elder writes that he does not wish to write “with pen and ink” but hopes to see his reader shortly and “speak face to face” (3 John 13–14). The parallel is one reason the two letters are usually assigned to the same writer.

reflections.title: Mouth to Mouth
reflections.html: “Though I have many things to write to you, I do not want to do so with paper and ink; but I hope to come to you and speak face to face.” The Greek says “mouth to mouth,” the phrase God used of His unique friendship with Moses: “I speak with him mouth to mouth” (Numbers 12:8). “Paper” is papyrus, used only here in the New Testament, a fragile sheet of reed strips; “ink” is literally “black,” a mixture of soot, gum, and water. The whole letter could fit on one sheet of papyrus, yet John wants for this church the kind of speaking God gave His friend Moses. God’s goal with His people has always been intimacy, not just information.
reflections.q: “Though I have many things to write to you, I do not want to do so with paper and ink; but I hope to come to you and speak face to face.”

reflections.title: Never Write When You Could Speak
reflections.html: Some things are better spoken than written. Church leaders and Christian people would do well to resolve never to write when they could speak. A page cannot carry a face, a tone, tears, or the chance to answer a question, and letters often harden what a conversation could have healed. John still had “many things” to say, and he saved them for the room. Hard conversations belong in person whenever possible (Matthew 18:15), and so do the tender ones. Is there a conversation we have been trying to handle by text or email that God wants us to have face to face?
reflections.q: Is there a conversation we have been trying to handle by text or email that God wants us to have face to face?

reflections.title: What We Send, We No Longer Control
reflections.html: John’s reason for setting down his pen applies with new force to texting and social media. A sent message can be forwarded, screenshotted, or resurfaced years after the moment that produced it, and the writer rarely controls where it travels next. Writing also cannot carry tone; sarcasm, humor, and correction read very differently on a screen than they sound in a voice. Email and messaging serve ordinary information well; they rarely serve correction, conflict, or anything carrying strong emotion. The wiser course is often to wait until the emotion has cooled, and sometimes the wisest of all is to stop typing and go speak with the person.
reflections.q: John’s reason for setting down his pen applies with new force to texting and social media.

reflections.title: The Limits of Paper and Ink
reflections.html: Even under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, John recognizes the limits of mediated communication. Information can travel on paper; spiritual impartation and human communion need presence. Even inspired apostolic writing is a poor substitute for being there, and true fellowship requires physical presence that no letter, and no modern medium, can replace.
reflections.q: Even under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, John recognizes the limits of mediated communication.

reflections.title: Joy Made Full Face to Face
reflections.html: “That your joy may be made full.” The phrase means joy brought to completion and kept full, the same words that close the opening of 1 John (1:4; compare John 15:11; 17:13). Joy is partial while we are apart; complete joy is relational and embodied. This mirrors the believer’s ultimate hope. We now have the “paper and ink” of Scripture, which brings us immense joy, and the written Word points us to living encounter with the Word made flesh. But our joy will only be made completely full when we see Christ face to face (1 Corinthians 13:12). Until then, the fullness of Christ is not known in isolation but in the gathered, face-to-face body, and nothing substitutes for face-to-face intimacy, whether with other believers or with God in the secret place.
reflections.q: “That your joy may be made full.”

reflections.title: Joy Was Never Meant to Be Virtual
reflections.html: John wants to see this church face to face so their joy may be full, a desire that reaches back to how people were made. Humanity was created for relationship with God and with each other, and some of life’s deepest joy is relational. That joy has been under attack since Eden: Adam and Eve hid after they sinned, and people have been finding reasons to hide ever since, fear, shame, old wounds, or simple busyness. Digital connection can imitate relationship without delivering it, leaving people who message often but rarely sit across a table with anyone still lonely. The fullness John longs for is found the way it has always been found: in the room, with the people God has placed around us.
reflections.q: John wants to see this church face to face so their joy may be full, a desire that reaches back to how people were made.

13.brief: The letter closes with greetings from “the children of your elect sister,” most naturally the members of the church where the Elder is, sending their love to a sister congregation. The family language that opened the letter returns at its end, and the “Amen” seals it.
13.explain:
“The children of your elect sister”

The letter opened with “the elect lady and her children” (verse 1), and it closes with her “elect sister” and her children. The two figures frame the letter. If the lady is a congregation, the elect sister is most naturally the church where the Elder was when he wrote, and her children are its members. If the lady is an individual Christian woman, these would be her nephews and nieces, apparently living near the Elder.

Like the lady, the sister is “elect,” chosen by God. Both owe their place in God’s family to the same God, which is why the Elder can call them sisters. Peter closes a letter in a similar way: “She who is in Babylon, elect together with you, greets you” (1 Peter 5:13). Christians in different cities were not strangers to one another. They were members of one family, children of the same Father.

“greet you. Amen.”

This greeting stands in deliberate contrast to the warning a few verses earlier. The readers were not to “greet” a teacher who denied that Jesus Christ came in the flesh (verse 10), because “he who greets him shares in his evil deeds” (verse 11). Here a greeting passes freely between two families of believers who share the same truth about Christ. A Christian greeting expresses fellowship, so it is withheld from those working against the truth and gladly given to those who hold it. Until the Elder could come and speak face to face (verse 12), this greeting carried the love of one church to another, and the “Amen” closes the letter.
13.notes: The “you” in “greet you” is singular in Greek, matching the singular address to the lady in verses 4–5.

reflections.title: Greetings From a Chosen Sister
reflections.html: “The children of your chosen sister greet you.” The letter that opened with a “chosen lady” closes with a “chosen sister,” so “chosen” frames the whole letter. If these are churches, the sister is likely John’s own congregation, probably at Ephesus; congregations are sisters and their members cousins in one family, sending greetings across the miles, sisters in the election of grace, keeping watch over one another. There are many local churches but one body of Christ sharing one divine life, a family that stretches across every border. The greetings of the New Testament are not polite filler; they are the arteries through which the lifeblood of Christian solidarity flows. In a letter that has just forbidden one greeting (v. 10), John ends by passing along another; the closed door of verse 10 did not make the church closed. No local church is an orphan, and none should live as if it were; we are never fighting the battle alone. Greet other churches, pray for them by name, and remember that the same Father chose them too.
reflections.q: “The children of your chosen sister greet you.”

reflections.title: The Shortest Book
reflections.html: With thirteen verses, 2 John has fewer verses than any other book of the Bible. (The greeting here is a different word from the forbidden “greeting” of verses 10–11: “embrace” rather than “rejoice.”)
reflections.q: With thirteen verses, 2 John has fewer verses than any other book of the Bible. (The greeting here is a different word from the forbidden “greeting” of verses 10–11: “embrace” rather than “rejoice.”)
